title: Median voter theorem

definition.text: The median voter theorem says that when voters and candidates line up along one left-right spectrum, majority-rule voting elects the candidate the middle (median) voter prefers.

facts.text: Voters are assumed to rank candidates by closeness; the candidate nearest the median voter then beats every rival by a majority.
Duncan Black first derived it in 1948, and Kenneth Arrow independently.
With two candidates a simple majority vote satisfies it; with more, any Condorcet method does.
In more than one dimension there may be no majority winner, as the McKelvey–Schofield chaos theorem shows.
It is popular in political economy because it yields testable links between voter characteristics and policy outcomes.
Levitt (1996) found senators from the same state but different parties voted only slightly more alike than random pairs, contradicting the theorem.

contested_note: Empirical studies from the US Senate and India find voting outcomes that contradict the theorem's predictions.

definition.text: The Hotelling–Downs model predicts that politicians who care only about winning will move to the median voter's position.

facts.text: It adapts Hotelling's 1929 principle of minimum differentiation in business competition, applied to politics by Anthony Downs in 1957.
In a two-party system it predicts both parties drift toward the median voter.
Primaries and most voting rules in national use break the conditions, so candidates may not converge.

title: Path dependence

definition.text: Path dependence is when past events or decisions constrain later ones, so that 'history matters' for where a system ends up.

facts.text: Economists developed it to explain how technologies are adopted and industries evolve.
A path-dependent process may settle into one of several equilibria depending on its starting point and chance events, unlike simple neoclassical models with one outcome.
Paul David argued in 1985 that a first-to-market standard such as the QWERTY keyboard can become entrenched even if inferior.
More than half the world's railways use the 143.5 cm standard gauge, inherited from early coal tramways.
Drivers include lock-in, positive feedback, increasing returns and self-reinforcement.
Commercial fisheries' harvest rates have been found to be path dependent, because institutions adapt slowly while ecosystems change fast.
Liebowitz and Margolis argue that inefficient lock-in is rare and that no real-world private cases exist.

contested_note: Economists still argue whether cases like QWERTY show real inefficient lock-in.

definition.text: A critical juncture is a moment when contingent choices set an institution on a path of development that is hard to reverse.

facts.text: Ruth and David Collier made the framework prominent in political science.
It has been used to explain the rise and persistence of welfare states and differences in economic development between countries.
Kathleen Thelen warns such frameworks are too deterministic, since institutions keep evolving.
